segments.title: What makes someone a historian?
segments.summary: Formal qualifications are optional when the work meets serious research and source standards and passes its findings on to others.
segments.body: Historical practice provides the test. A historian researches carefully, handles sources responsibly, and passes on what the work reveals. Academic qualifications can show that someone has learned those standards. Academic historians should also, in theory, have experienced the blunt challenge of "you're wrong, prove you're not," with references and a research record used to defend their case. In naval and military history, academics form only a small share of the field, and non-academic historians bring different perspectives and often provide the toughest conference questioning. That experience is specific to these fields, since other areas of history may operate differently, and disagreement should stay focused on the thesis instead of personal attacks. Qualifications are most relevant for someone who wants to teach at a university; responsible historical work does not otherwise require them.
segments.question: Does someone need academic qualifications to be a historian, and what distinguishes academic from non-academic historians?
segments.answerShort: No. Qualifications are most relevant to university teaching. In this view, serious research and responsible use of sources make the historian, and naval and military history show how non-academics can bring sharp criticism and different perspectives to the field.

evidence.note: He contrasts qualifications with research and source standards, explains academic debate, and uses naval and military history to describe rigorous non-academic participation.
